templates.pattern: A habitat has [N] individuals of a species spread over an area of [A] km². Calculate the population density (individuals per km²).
templates.explanation:
Population Density = Number of individuals ÷ Area
= [N] ÷ [A]
= [RESULT] individuals/km²

Population density tells us how crowded a species is within its habitat. Higher values indicate more individuals per unit area.

templates.pattern: A field survey counted [N] individuals in a [A] m² quadrat. What is the population density in individuals per m²?
templates.explanation:
Population Density = Number of individuals ÷ Area
= [N] ÷ [A]
= [RESULT] individuals/m²

Quadrat sampling is commonly used in ecology to estimate population density of plants or slow-moving animals.

templates.pattern: Producers at trophic level 1 contain [E] kJ of energy. Using the 10% rule, how much energy (kJ) is available at trophic level 3?
templates.explanation:
10% Rule: only 10% of energy passes from one trophic level to the next.
Level 1 → Level 2: [E] × 0.10
Level 2 → Level 3: [E] × 0.10 × 0.10 = [E] × 0.01
= [RESULT] kJ

Energy is lost as heat, movement, and waste at each level.

templates.pattern: Producers contain [E] kJ of energy. Using the 10% rule, how much energy (kJ) is available at trophic level 2?
templates.explanation:
10% Rule: Energy at trophic level 2 = Energy at level 1 × 10%
= [E] × 0.10
= [RESULT] kJ

Primary consumers (herbivores) receive only 10% of the energy stored in producers.

templates.pattern: In a food chain, producers have a biomass of [P] kg. Secondary consumers have a biomass of [S] kg. How many trophic levels separate them if the 10% efficiency rule applies? (Express as a whole number.)
templates.explanation:
Using the 10% rule: Biomass_n = Biomass_1 × (0.1)^(n-1)
[S] = [P] × (0.1)^(n-1)
(0.1)^(n-1) = [S]/[P]
(n-1) = log10([P]/[S])
n-1 = [RESULT]-1 levels apart

This tells us how many transfer steps separate the two trophic levels.

templates.pattern: A food chain has [TL] trophic levels. Producers contain [E] kJ of energy. Using the 10% rule, how much energy (kJ) reaches the top trophic level?
templates.explanation:
Energy at top = E × (0.1)^(TL − 1)
= [E] × (0.1)^([TL] − 1)
= [RESULT] kJ

The longer the food chain, the less energy reaches the top predator. This is why most food chains have only 4–5 levels.

templates.pattern: In an ecosystem, there are [PRED] predators and [PREY] prey animals. What is the predator-to-prey ratio (round to 2 decimal places)?
templates.explanation:
Predator-to-Prey ratio = Number of predators ÷ Number of prey
= [PRED] ÷ [PREY]
= [RESULT]

This ratio is typically much less than 1, meaning prey far outnumber predators. A healthy ecosystem requires enough prey to support the predator population.

templates.pattern: A sample plot of [A] m² contains [S] different species. What is the species richness per m²?
templates.explanation:
Species Richness per unit area = Number of species ÷ Area
= [S] ÷ [A]
= [RESULT] species/m²

Species richness is a simple measure of biodiversity — the more species in a given area, the higher the richness.

templates.pattern: A population has [B] births and [D] deaths in one year. What is the net population growth for that year?
templates.explanation:
Population Growth = Births − Deaths
= [B] − [D]
= [RESULT] individuals

This is the simplest model of population change (ignoring immigration and emigration). A positive value means the population is growing.

templates.pattern: Plants in an ecosystem fix [GPP] kJ/m²/yr of energy through photosynthesis and use [R] kJ/m²/yr for respiration. What is the Net Primary Production (NPP) in kJ/m²/yr?
templates.explanation:
Net Primary Production (NPP) = Gross Primary Production (GPP) − Respiration (R)
= [GPP] − [R]
= [RESULT] kJ/m²/yr

NPP represents the energy actually available to consumers in the ecosystem. It is the energy stored in plant biomass after the plant's own metabolic needs are met.
